Along the way we pick up the S3 features you’d want in a real upload/download path (presigned URLs, streaming, versioning, lifecycle rules), and we write the series’ first async code, because moving file bytes is the first place in this app where async is worth the trouble. What we will cover in this part Simple (PutObject) vs multipart upload, and why we let boto3’s transfer manager choose Presigned URLs: a time-limited, signed URL that lets a client fetch from S3 directly instead of going through our API Streaming responses, so a large document never has to sit fully in memory Versioning and lifecycle rules at the bucket level Path-style vs virtual-hosted-style addressing, and why MiniStack needs the former Converting the upload/download path to aioboto3, and when that’s worth doing Prerequisites The Part 2 skeleton, running (make up, make seed, make run, and /config returns the resolved config) Two new Python packages: aioboto3 (an async boto3) and python-multipart (FastAPI needs it to parse file uploads) No new MiniStack services. S3 has been listening on port 4566 since Part 1. Concepts Simple upload vs multipart upload S3 gives you two ways to upload. PutObject sends the whole object in one HTTP request, which is fine when you already have all the bytes in memory anyway. Multipart upload splits the object into parts (CreateMultipartUpload, then a series of UploadPart calls, then CompleteMultipartUpload). You’re forced into multipart above 5 GB, but it’s useful well below that: parts can upload in parallel, and if one part fails you retry just that part instead of re-sending the whole file. The good news is that we don’t have to write any of this. upload_fileobj looks at the object’s size and switches to multipart above a threshold (8 MB by default). It’s the same call whether the document is a 40 KB text file or a 400 MB PDF, and I see no reason to reimplement something s3transfer already gets right. Presigned URLs A presigned URL is an ordinary S3 URL with a signature and an expiry baked into the query string. Generating one (generate_presigned_url) doesn’t touch the network at all; it’s an HMAC computed locally with credentials we already have. Whoever holds the URL can do exactly one operation on one key until it expires. Why bother? Without presigned URLs, every byte of every document passes through our FastAPI process twice, once on the way in and once on the way out. With them, the client talks to S3 directly and our API only ever ships small JSON responses. For a document-heavy app that’s a big difference in what the API server has to be sized for. Streaming responses The obvious way to serve a download is to call get_object, read the whole body into memory, and return it as bytes. That’s fine for a 5 KB metadata file. For a 200-page contract it means the full document sits in RAM for the length of the request, once per concurrent download. StreamingResponse takes an iterator instead of a value, so bytes flow from S3 through our process to the client in chunks, and the complete document never exists in our memory at any one moment. Versioning and lifecycle rules Turn versioning on for a bucket and overwrites stop being destructive. S3 keeps the old body as a noncurrent version and makes the new one current; GetObject without a VersionId still returns the current version, so none of the download code has to change. It’s a safety net against accidental overwrites and deletes that just sits underneath everything. One thing that surprised me when I first ran into it: you can’t fully turn versioning off again. You can suspend a versioned bucket, but it never goes back to “never versioned.” Lifecycle rules are the other half. They’re bucket-level policies that act on objects automatically: expire them after N days, transition them to cheaper storage classes, and so on. The one we set up below expires noncurrent versions after 30 days, because otherwise versioning quietly becomes an unbounded storage bill. Path-style vs virtual-hosted-style addressing Real S3 supports two URL shapes for the same object: virtual-hosted-style (https://inbox-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com/<key>, bucket name as a DNS subdomain) and path-style (https://s3.amazonaws.com/inbox-uploads/<key>, bucket name as a path segment). AWS has been steering everyone toward virtual-hosted-style for years, but it depends on DNS resolving inbox-uploads.s3.amazonaws.com. Nothing on your laptop is going to resolve inbox-uploads.localhost:4566, so for MiniStack we tell boto3 to use path-style: from botocore.config import Config Config(s3={"addressing_style": "path"}) This matters mostly for presigned URLs. Get the addressing style wrong and the signed URL points at a host that doesn’t exist, so the request hangs or fails to connect before MiniStack ever sees it. There’s no helpful signature error, because the signature never gets checked. I lost a good half hour to this the first time; there’s an entry in Troubleshooting for it. Build The target layout after this part (new/changed files marked): docinbox/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py # + async S3 client in lifespan, /documents endpoints │ ├── config.py # unchanged │ ├── app_config.py # unchanged │ └── aws/ │ ├── clients.py # unchanged — still used by /healthz, /whoami, bootstrap │ └── aclients.py # NEW: the async client factory (aioboto3) ├── bootstrap/ │ └── seed.py # + seed_bucket: create bucket, enable versioning, lifecycle rule ├── docker-compose.yml # unchanged — S3_PERSIST=1 was already set in Part 1 ├── requirements.txt # + aioboto3, python-multipart └── ... 1. New dependencies requirements.txt gains two lines: aioboto3>=13.0 python-multipart>=0.0.9 pip install -r requirements.txt Note that python-multipart is not optional. FastAPI raises at import time if a route declares UploadFile and the package is missing. 2. The async client factory Part 1’s get_client() stays exactly as it is. /healthz, /whoami, and bootstrap/seed.py keep using it, since none of those do enough I/O for async to matter. What we add is an async counterpart, used only where we’re about to move real document bytes. aioboto3 clients differ from boto3 clients in one important way: they hold an open aiohttp session, so they have to be used as an async context manager (async with session.client(...) as s3:) rather than constructed once and cached as a bare object the way get_client caches a boto3.client. The natural place to open one for the lifetime of the app is the FastAPI lifespan, with an AsyncExitStack to make sure it closes on shutdown. app/aws/aclients.py: """The async counterpart to clients.py — for the I/O worth overlapping. boto3 clients (clients.py) are cheap to cache and reuse everywhere. aioboto3 clients hold an open aiohttp session and must be opened as an async context manager, so this module hands one out tied to an AsyncExitStack the caller owns (in practice: the app lifespan). """ from contextlib import AsyncExitStack from typing import Any import aioboto3 from botocore.config import Config from app.config import get_settings # Path-style addressing: with the virtual-hosted default, a presigned URL # would point at http://inbox-uploads.localhost:4566/..., which nothing # resolves. Path-style keeps the bucket name in the path instead. _S3_ADDRESSING = Config(s3={"addressing_style": "path"}) _session = aioboto3.Session() def _client_kwargs() -> dict[str, Any]: settings = get_settings() kwargs: dict[str, Any] = { "region_name": settings.aws_region, "aws_access_key_id": settings.aws_access_key_id, "aws_secret_access_key": settings.aws_secret_access_key, "config": _S3_ADDRESSING, } if settings.aws_endpoint_url: kwargs["endpoint_url"] = settings.aws_endpoint_url return kwargs async def open_async_client(stack: AsyncExitStack, service: str) -> Any: """Open an async client for `service`, tied to `stack`'s lifetime. Call this once (the app lifespan does) and reuse the client it returns — aioboto3 clients are not meant to be opened per request. """ return await stack.enter_async_context(_session.client(service, **_client_kwargs())) 3. Wiring it into the lifespan app/main.py (the lifespan grows; everything from Part 2 stays): from contextlib import AsyncExitStack, asynccontextmanager from app.aws.aclients import open_async_client @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): cache = ConfigCache(ttl_seconds=get_settings().config_ttl_seconds) cache.get() # fail-fast config load, from Part 2 app.state.config_cache = cache async with AsyncExitStack() as stack: app.state.s3 = await open_async_client(stack, "s3") yield # the stack closes app.state.s3's aiohttp session on shutdown app.state.s3 is now a live async S3 client for the whole life of the process: one aiohttp session shared across every request, instead of one opened and closed per call. 4. Uploading a document import uuid from fastapi import Depends, File, HTTPException, UploadFile from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse @app.post("/documents", status_code=201) async def upload_document( file: UploadFile = File(...), config: AppConfig = Depends(get_app_config), ) -> dict[str, str]: """Upload a document to S3. The document id is a new key, not the filename.""" document_id = str(uuid.uuid4()) content_type = file.content_type or "application/octet-stream" # upload_fileobj picks simple vs multipart based on size — we don't. await app.state.s3.upload_fileobj( file.file, config.bucket_name, document_id, ExtraArgs={ "ContentType": content_type, "Metadata": {"filename": file.filename or "unnamed"}, }, ) return {"document_id": document_id, "filename": file.filename, "content_type": content_type} The key is a fresh UUID rather than the original filename. That way two people uploading invoice.pdf don’t collide, though it does mean we need somewhere to remember what a given id is. For now that somewhere is the object’s own S3 metadata. Part 4 replaces this with a proper DynamoDB record. file.file is FastAPI’s SpooledTemporaryFile (small uploads stay in memory, large ones spill to disk on their own), and we hand it straight to upload_fileobj rather than reading it into a bytes first. Reading it fully up front would work fine for a demo, but it would also throw away most of what this section is trying to accomplish. 5. Listing documents We don’t have a database yet, so “list documents” means asking S3 what’s in the bucket. This is a placeholder that Part 4 replaces with a real query: @app.get("/documents") async def list_documents(config: AppConfig = Depends(get_app_config)) -> dict[str, list[dict]]: resp = await app.state.s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket=config.bucket_name) documents = [ { "document_id": obj["Key"], "size": obj["Size"], "last_modified": obj["LastModified"].isoformat(), } for obj in resp.get("Contents", []) ] return {"documents": documents} 6. Downloading a document — streamed from botocore.exceptions import ClientError @app.get("/documents/{document_id}/download") async def download_document( document_id: str, config: AppConfig = Depends(get_app_config), ) -> StreamingResponse: try: obj = await app.state.s3.get_object(Bucket=config.bucket_name, Key=document_id) except app.state.s3.exceptions.NoSuchKey as exc: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="document not found") from exc filename = obj.get("Metadata", {}).get("filename", document_id) headers = {"Content-Disposition": f'attachment; filename="{filename}"'} if "ContentLength" in obj: headers["Content-Length"] = str(obj["ContentLength"]) return StreamingResponse( obj["Body"].iter_chunks(), media_type=obj.get("ContentType", "application/octet-stream"), headers=headers, ) obj["Body"] from an aioboto3 response is an async streaming body, and iter_chunks() gives you an async generator of byte chunks, which happens to be exactly the shape StreamingResponse wants. At no point does the whole document exist as a single bytes object in our process. 7. Downloading a document — presigned URL The streamed route works, but every byte still passes through our API process. The alternative is to hand the client a presigned URL and let it fetch from S3 directly. @app.get("/documents/{document_id}/download-url") async def download_document_url( document_id: str, config: AppConfig = Depends(get_app_config), ) -> dict[str, str | int]: # HeadObject confirms the key exists before we hand out a URL for it. try: await app.state.s3.head_object(Bucket=config.bucket_name, Key=document_id) except ClientError as exc: if exc.response["Error"]["Code"] == "404": raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="document not found") from exc raise url = await app.state.s3.generate_presigned_url( "get_object", Params={"Bucket": config.bucket_name, "Key": document_id}, ExpiresIn=300, ) return {"url": url, "expires_in": 300} Two small things worth noting. First, generate_presigned_url gets await-ed here even though signing does no network I/O; aioboto3 wraps every client method as a coroutine for consistency, and this one just returns immediately. Second, the 300-second expiry is short on purpose. A presigned URL works for anyone who has it, so the window should be just long enough for the client to start the download. 8. Seeding the bucket: versioning + lifecycle Until now the bucket has only ever been created by hand. Time to fold it into the same idempotent bootstrap/seed.py from Part 2, alongside the parameters and the secret. We reuse the bucket name already defined in PARAMETERS, so the config and the seed script can’t drift apart: def seed_bucket(env: str) -> None: s3 = get_client("s3") bucket = PARAMETERS["s3/bucket-name"] try: s3.create_bucket(Bucket=bucket) print(f" bucket {bucket} (created)") except s3.exceptions.BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou: print(f" bucket {bucket} (already exists, kept)") s3.put_bucket_versioning(Bucket=bucket, VersioningConfiguration={"Status": "Enabled"}) s3.put_bucket_lifecycle_configuration( Bucket=bucket, LifecycleConfiguration={ "Rules": [ { "ID": "expire-noncurrent-versions", "Status": "Enabled", "Filter": {"Prefix": ""}, "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {"NoncurrentDays": 30}, } ] }, ) print(f" bucket {bucket}: versioning enabled, lifecycle rule applied") def main() -> None: env = get_settings().app_env print(f"Seeding docinbox resources for env '{env}'...") seed_parameters(env) seed_signing_key(env) seed_bucket(env) print("Done.") The bucket gets the same create-only-if-missing treatment as the secret in Part 2, so re-running the seed script won’t fail just because the bucket already exists. put_bucket_versioning and put_bucket_lifecycle_configuration don’t need any of that: they’re declarative sets, and calling them again simply reasserts the same configuration. 9. The full loop make up # MiniStack make seed # parameters + secret (Part 2) + bucket, versioning, lifecycle (this part) make run # app — opens the async S3 client in the lifespan Upload a document and note its id: curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/documents -F "file=@contract.pdf;type=application/pdf" | jq . # { # "document_id": "6f1a9e2e-...-...", # "filename": "contract.pdf", # "content_type": "application/pdf" # } List it, download it streamed, and diff the result against the original: curl -s localhost:8000/documents | jq . # {"documents":[{"document_id":"6f1a9e2e-...","size":48213,"last_modified":"2026-07-20T..."}]} curl -s localhost:8000/documents/6f1a9e2e-.../download -o out.pdf diff contract.pdf out.pdf && echo "identical" # identical Now the presigned route. Note that the second curl below talks straight to MiniStack: curl -s localhost:8000/documents/6f1a9e2e-.../download-url | jq . # {"url":"http://localhost:4566/inbox-uploads/6f1a9e2e-...?X-Amz-Algorithm=...","expires_in":300} curl -s "http://localhost:4566/inbox-uploads/6f1a9e2e-...?X-Amz-Algorithm=..." -o out2.pdf diff contract.pdf out2.pdf && echo "identical, and our API process never touched these bytes" You could kill the FastAPI process entirely at this point and that second curl would still work, since it never touches our API. Try it if you don’t believe me. Versioning, on a separate manual key (so we don’t need to reuse a real document id to see it): echo "v1" | aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 s3 cp - s3://inbox-uploads/demo.txt echo "v2" | aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 s3 cp - s3://inbox-uploads/demo.txt aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 s3api list-object-versions \ --bucket inbox-uploads --prefix demo.txt --query "Versions[].{Id:VersionId,Latest:IsLatest}" # [ # {"Id": "null" or a real version id, "Latest": true}, # {"Id": "...", "Latest": false} # ] Two versions of the same key now exist, and GET /documents, which always reads the current version, is unaffected. Finally, persistence. S3_PERSIST=1 has been set since Part 1, but this is the first time we have bytes worth losing: docker compose restart ministack curl -s localhost:8000/documents | jq . # the same document is still listed — the object survived the restart The general pattern The portable version of this, if you’re building something else: an endpoint that moves bytes to and from an object store shouldn’t default to proxying everything through your API. Offer a presigned-URL path for large transfers. Stream rather than buffer on whatever side does go through your process. And reach for an async client at the specific boundary where a blocking call would sit on a thread-pool worker for the whole transfer, rather than rewriting code that was working fine synchronously. In production We put put_bucket_versioning and put_bucket_lifecycle_configuration in a seed script because it’s convenient locally. In a real deployment that’s Terraform or CloudFormation’s job. The app shouldn’t be mutating its own bucket’s config at runtime. The 300-second presigned expiry isn’t just a round number I picked; production systems usually go tighter. Whatever you choose, scope the URL to one key and one operation. Never a prefix, never a wildcard. Tune the multipart threshold once you know your real traffic. 8 MB is a fine general default, but on a fast, high-latency link, dropping it via TransferConfig lets more parts upload in parallel, and that can be a real throughput win. Async pays off at concurrency. A blocking boto3 call sitting in FastAPI’s thread pool is fine at low volume; the trouble starts when you have enough concurrent uploads and downloads that the default pool size (40, for Uvicorn/Starlette) becomes the bottleneck rather than S3 itself. If you’re nowhere near that, honestly, the sync version is fine. MiniStack notes and fidelity S3_PERSIST=1 and the volume mounts from Part 1 are the whole reason the restart demo above works. Object bytes and bucket-level config both survive docker compose restart. If you’re relying on some more obscure piece of S3 metadata surviving a restart, don’t assume; go check. Path-style addressing is a hard requirement here, not a preference. Drop the Config(s3={"addressing_style": "path"}) and presigned URLs get signed for a virtual-hosted host that nothing on your machine resolves. As mentioned above, the failure mode is a connection failure with no useful error, and it’s annoying to debug the first time you hit it. Lifecycle rules have a timing gap worth knowing about. Real S3 evaluates them in a batch job that runs roughly once a day, so an Expiration of one day doesn’t mean the object disappears the moment the clock rolls over. Treat the lifecycle exercise below as a configuration exercise; watching it fire needs real AWS and more patience than a weekend gives you. No IAM enforcement, still, same as every part so far. Any caller can read or write anything in the bucket. Part 8 is where this gets fixed. Troubleshooting ImportError mentioning python-multipart when you hit /documents. The dependency from step 1 is missing. pip install -r requirements.txt. NoSuchBucket on upload. You probably pulled this part’s changes but didn’t re-run make seed. Run it, then sanity-check with aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566 s3 ls. The presigned URL 404s or connects to the wrong host. This is the addressing-style problem: either the Config from step 2 got dropped, or you copied a URL that was generated before that change went in. Re-request /documents/{id}/download-url and look at the host in the returned URL. It should be localhost:4566/inbox-uploads/..., not inbox-uploads.localhost:4566/.... RuntimeError: Session is closed on the second request after a hot-reload. uvicorn --reload restarted the app, and the async S3 client from the old lifespan went with it. This is normal during development; retry once the reload settles, or do a real restart. Downloaded file differs from the upload. Before assuming data corruption, check whether a client mangled line endings (usually a Content-Type/Content-Disposition mismatch). Compare with diff or sha256sum rather than eyeballing the file. Weekend exercises Presign an upload, not just a download. Add GET /documents/upload-url returning a presigned URL for put_object with a fresh document id, so a client can upload straight to S3 without the bytes ever reaching our API. Notice what breaks: the Metadata={"filename": ...} trick has nowhere to run anymore, since we never see the upload happen. Add server-side encryption. Drop "ServerSideEncryption": "AES256" into the ExtraArgs in upload_document, then confirm it took by checking the ServerSideEncryption field on a head_object response. Add a real expiration rule on objects under a tmp/ prefix, in addition to the noncurrent-version one. You won’t see it fire this weekend (see the fidelity note above about lifecycle timing), but it’s worth writing the rule correctly and noting it in the series’ fidelity appendix (coming at the end of the series) to check against real AWS someday. Force a multipart upload and go watch it happen. Pass TransferConfig(multipart_threshold=1024 * 1024) into upload_fileobj, upload something over 1 MB, and set LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG on the MiniStack container to watch the individual UploadPart calls scroll by. What is next docinbox can now take a document in and hand it back out, either streamed through the API or via a presigned URL that skips it entirely, with versioning and a lifecycle rule underneath. What it still can’t do is answer anything about who a document belongs to or what state it’s in. Right now “list documents” just means asking S3 what keys happen to exist, and that falls over the moment you want “show me Alice’s contracts.” Part 4 — The Data Layer: DynamoDB. We’ll design a single-table schema around docinbox’s real access patterns, build a typed repository on top of it, add a GSI for documents-by-owner, and leave room in the schema for the LLM-derived fields Part 7 will eventually populate. The list_objects_v2 placeholder from this part gets replaced with an actual query. The source code used in this part is available in the companion GitHub repository: github.com/chuan2019/docinbox (tag part-03). See you next weekend.

title: Observability of Modern AI Application Systems: Literature and Industry Landscape
tags: llm, observability, opentelemetry, agents, llmops, evaluation, literature-review
content: Compiled July 2026 (revised and expanded with industry coverage) 1. Introduction Over the past three years, large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents have been more and more widely adopted in production software systems. Along with this trend, a new engineering discipline has emerged at the intersection of classical distributed-systems observability, machine-learning monitoring, and AI evaluation research. Different from conventional software, AI application systems are non-deterministic and prompt-sensitive, and they fail in ways that produce no stack trace and no HTTP 500: hallucination, drift, prompt injection, silent tool failures, and so on. In order to understand why such a system misbehaved, we need telemetry that captures not only latency and errors, but also semantic content, including prompts, completions, retrieved context, tool invocations, reasoning steps, and quality scores. It should be noted that in this field, industry practice is running ahead of academic publication. Vendors, open-source projects, and engineering blogs did most of the work of defining the category between 2023 and 2026, and academic research has been catching up and formalizing it afterwards. A review restricted to peer-reviewed sources would therefore miss most of what actually happened. In this article, I am going to review both the literature and the current industry progress on observability of modern AI application systems. The article is organized as follows. Section 2 and Section 3 review the classical observability and ML-monitoring foundations on which the field is built. Section 4 and Section 5 describe how the problem space changed with LLM applications and how “LLM observability” became a product category. Section 6 summarizes the industry state of play as of mid-2026, including market dynamics and frontier practice. Section 7 and Section 8 review the academic work on evaluation and on agent observability. Section 9 and Section 10 cover the emerging standards and the regulatory drivers. Section 11 concludes with a synthesis and a list of open research gaps. As discussed above, industry takes an important lead in this field. Accordingly, following the convention of multivocal literature reviews, grey literature such as vendor whitepapers, engineering blogs, and arXiv preprints is included and flagged throughout the article. Consequently, the industry figures, in Section 6 in particular, should not be taken too literally. 2. Foundations: Observability in Distributed Systems Modern AI observability inherits most of its conceptual machinery from two decades of distributed-systems work. The trace/span model originates from Google’s Dapper [1], which demonstrated how to implement distributed tracing with low overhead, application-level transparency, and context propagation across RPC boundaries. Dapper is the direct ancestor of Zipkin, Jaeger, and eventually OpenTelemetry. The Google SRE book [40] contributed the “four golden signals”, i.e., latency, traffic, errors, and saturation, as the minimal metric set for any user-facing system, and Sridharan [41] popularized the “three pillars” framing of logs, metrics, and traces as complementary telemetry types. These threads were consolidated into OpenTelemetry (OTel), which was formed in 2019 from the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus, and graduated as a CNCF project in 2026. OTel provides the vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, and wire protocol (OTLP) that essentially all AI-observability tooling builds upon today. In addition, the W3C Trace Context recommendation [33] standardized the traceparent header for cross-service trace propagation. As we will see in Section 8.3, this mechanism becomes newly relevant, and also newly problematic, when agent-to-tool call chains traverse non-HTTP transports. The reason why this lineage transfers is straightforward: an LLM application is essentially a distributed system whose requests carry multi-kilobyte natural-language payloads. A RAG pipeline or an agent run maps naturally onto a span tree. What does not transfer is the assumption about payload size and content. As Traceloop’s founders put it, “nobody designed telemetry for multi-kilobyte prompts”. The AI-specific extensions surveyed in Section 9 are designed to fill this gap. 3. Pre-LLM Machine Learning Monitoring The second foundation is the ML-systems literature of 2015–2022, whose lasting contribution was to establish that deployed models fail in ways invisible to conventional monitoring. Sculley et al. [2], in the canonical “Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems”, argued that most of an ML system’s failure surface lies outside the model code: entanglement, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, and changes in the external world. Breck et al. [3] operationalized this into the ML Test Score, a rubric of 28 tests and monitoring needs drawn from Google’s production systems. Its monitoring section, which covers training/serving skew, feature staleness, and prediction-quality degradation, is arguably the first concrete checklist of what to observe in a deployed model. Breck et al. [4] subsequently described TFX’s data-validation system, which made continuous data-quality monitoring (schema validation, skew detection, and anomaly alerting) a standard component of production ML stacks. The statistical layer of model monitoring rests on the concept-drift literature, which was comprehensively surveyed by Lu et al. [5]. They frame the problem as three steps: (1) detection, (2) understanding, and (3) adaptation. Rabanser et al. [6] empirically benchmarked practical dataset-shift detection pipelines (dimensionality reduction plus two-sample tests) under the well-chosen title “Failing Loudly”. The title captures the point of the whole subfield: ML systems fail silently by default, and the purpose of monitoring is to make them fail loudly. Klaise et al. [7] connected this research to deployable architecture, and described a production stack consisting of performance monitoring, outlier detection, drift detection, and prediction explanation. Huyen [42] provides the standard textbook treatment of the drift taxonomy (covariate shift, label shift, and concept drift) and the corresponding detection statistics. Shankar and Parameswaran [8] were among the first to use “observability” as an explicit framing for ML. They proposed a bolt-on data-management system supporting detection, diagnosis, and reaction to ML bugs under delayed or missing labels. The distinction they draw is useful: monitoring means passively watching dashboards for known failure modes, while observability means being able to interrogate the system about novel ones. A companion interview study [9] documented that practitioners experience production ML as a continual loop of experimentation, evaluation, and monitoring, and that monitoring is the dominant pain point. As one interviewee put it, “we have no idea how models will behave in production until production”. Finally, Kreuzberger et al. [10] produced the canonical definition and reference architecture of MLOps via a mixed-method study, in which monitoring and continuous feedback loops are among the core principles. This lifecycle framing carries forward into LLMOps, which we discuss next. 4. From MLOps to LLMOps: The New Problem Space The arrival of foundation-model applications changed the monitoring problem qualitatively, not just in degree. Classical ML monitoring assumes a fixed model, structured features, and ground-truth labels that eventually arrive. In contrast, LLM applications have prompt-driven behavior, unbounded text I/O, third-party API-served models with no access to internals, and, for open-ended generation, no ground truth at all. There is empirical documentation of the resulting gaps. Xia et al. [19] analyzed over 29,000 questions from the OpenAI developer forum to build a taxonomy of LLM application-development challenges, in which debugging and monitoring difficulties figure prominently. A practitioner-view synthesis [20] reached a similar conclusion: prompt sensitivity and few-shot behavior create monitoring and evaluation concerns that traditional ML tooling does not address. An emerging LLMOps literature extends the lifecycle of Kreuzberger et al. [10] with prompt management, cost/latency monitoring, and continuous evaluation as additional lifecycle stages, though this strand has not yet landed in top venues. The most influential problem statements of the period came out of industry practice. Carter’s “All the Hard Stuff Nobody Talks About when Building Products with LLMs” [46], written after shipping one of the first production LLM features, enumerated six hard problems (context windows, prompt engineering, latency, correctness, security, and compliance), and argued that non-deterministic LLM features have to be debugged from real user telemetry, because offline testing cannot cover the input space. Majors and Carter [47] added another important point: models cannot be understood in isolation from the surrounding software system, so AI observability presupposes good observability of everything else. Carter’s O’Reilly report Observability for Large Language Models [43] is the first book-length treatment. Its core idea is to close a production feedback loop, i.e., to capture user behavior, performance, and feedback as OpenTelemetry data, and use it to refine prompts and evals systematically. Huyen’s AI Engineering [44] gives the corresponding textbook chapter, and is notable for treating user feedback, both explicit and conversational, as a telemetry signal in its own right. 5. LLM Observability as a Product Category Between 2023 and 2026, “LLM observability” became a product category. The vendor literature is promotional, of course, but it did much of the definitional work, and it is where the shared vocabulary comes from. A consistent signal set emerged across vendors: (1) traces and spans of LLM calls, retrievals, and tool invocations; (2) token usage, cost, and latency per call and per user or feature; (3) full prompt/response payload logging; (4) evaluation scores computed online, using LLM-as-judge and code-based scorers; (5) human feedback and annotations; (6) drift over prompts, topics, and embeddings; and (7) safety signals such as toxicity, PII exposure, prompt injection, and guardrail violations. Arize’s “LLM Observability 101” whitepaper [48] organized an early version of this into “five pillars”. Braintrust’s guides [50] state the formula that has since become standard: observability is tracing plus evals plus monitoring, over shared data. On the capture side, three instrumentation architectures recur. The first is SDK/decorator instrumentation (LangSmith, Langfuse, and W&B Weave, whose @weave.op decorator yields automatic hierarchical call trees), which embeds tracing in the application code. The second is proxy/gateway interception (Helicone), which routes LLM traffic through a logging gateway. This approach is architecturally simple, but it couples observability to the request path. The third is OTel-native auto-instrumentation (OpenLLMetry, OpenLIT, and HoneyHive), which patches provider SDKs to emit standard OTLP, and therefore decouples instrumentation from the backend. All three approaches now converge on OTel semantics as the interoperability layer, as we will see in Section 9. I will not catalogue every platform here; the ones below each introduced an idea that stuck. LangSmith (from LangChain) established the idea that the same traces powering observability should also power evaluation, with annotation queues for human labeling [51]. This trace-to-eval-dataset loop is now the standard workflow everywhere. Langfuse [55] became the leading open-source, self-hostable implementation, with native OTLP ingestion. Galileo closed the loop from evaluation to enforcement, by running research-backed metrics via small purpose-trained judge models fast enough (sub-200ms) that they can block bad outputs in production instead of just scoring them afterwards. TruLens introduced the RAG Triad (context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance) [54], a reference-free framework for RAG failure modes which has been widely copied. In addition, Arize/Phoenix carried the pre-LLM drift rigor into embedding-drift detection; WhyLabs LangKit typifies the “metrics-from-text” approach of extracting quality and safety signals from payloads; and DeepEval/Confident AI framed evaluation as unit testing wired into CI. The APM incumbents then mainstreamed the category. Datadog’s LLM Observability [49] reached general availability in 2024 with span-level input/output capture, token/cost tracking, online hallucination/toxicity/injection evaluations, and topic-drift detection, and has since been renamed toward “Agent Observability” with native adoption of the OTel GenAI conventions. New Relic and Dynatrace ship comparable capabilities inside classical APM. The second edition of Observability Engineering [45], which was substantially rewritten “for an AI world” and includes chapters on debugging LLM applications in production, marks the point where AI observability was absorbed into the observability canon. 6. Industry State of Play, 2025–2026 The previous section describes what the category is. This section describes where the industry actually stands as of mid-2026. Again, the sources here are almost entirely grey: market reports, press releases, and vendor blogs [57–65]. Individual numbers deserve skepticism, but the aggregate picture is consistent across enough independent sources, so the overall trend should be reliable even if the figures are not. 6.1 Market maturation and consolidation AI observability has become a budgeted line item. Market analyses put the segment at roughly $1.1B in 2025, inside an overall observability market growing toward the tens of billions, and one 2026 estimate puts the agent-observability slice alone at around $2.2B [59, 60]. These figures should be treated as rough estimates only, since the category boundaries differ from report to report. The M&A record is a clearer signal, and the 2025–2026 period produced a lot of it: ClickHouse acquired Langfuse (January 2026) as part of a $400M Series D, folding the most widely adopted open-source LLM-engineering platform into a columnar-database company [59]. The implied thesis is that LLM traces are fundamentally an analytical-database workload. OpenAI acquired promptfoo (March 2026), pulling the leading open-source red-teaming and eval framework into a frontier lab’s own infrastructure [62]. To the best of my knowledge, this is the first case where a frontier lab vertically integrated evaluation tooling that had grown up in the open-source ecosystem. Classical observability consolidated in parallel: Palo Alto Networks acquired Chronosphere, Snowflake announced the acquisition of Observe, and LogicMonitor bought Catchpoint [58]. In other words, security and data-platform vendors are buying their way into telemetry, on the theory that whoever holds the operational data will end up hosting the operational agents. Datadog, at roughly $3.3B revenue in 2025, kept expanding by acquisition (Eppo for experimentation, Metaplane for data observability), and positions LLM/agent observability as one pane among many [59]. Earlier, Helicone was acquired and moved to maintenance mode, which suggests that standalone proxy-based LLM logging does not survive as an independent business. Several industry analyses (e.g., Splunk’s 2026 trends piece [58]) read the pattern in the same way: pure-play monitoring vendors face pricing pressure as their traditional use cases get automated away, and the buyers are platforms that can consolidate data across domains and let customers run agents over it. Accordingly, the market appears to be deciding that AI observability is a feature of data platforms, and that the standalone category may not survive. Anyone building or researching in this space should factor that in. 6.2 The open-source and self-hosted stack Alongside the commercial platforms, there is a healthy open-source ecosystem, which is sustained mainly by teams with data-residency, compliance, or cost constraints. Note that the privacy tension discussed in Section 11 is a real adoption driver here, since self-hosting is currently the main practical answer to it. The 2026 self-hosted landscape splits into two camps [64]. The first camp is the LLM-native platforms: Langfuse (MIT-licensed core, now ClickHouse-backed), Arize Phoenix (OTel-native via OpenInference, ELv2 license), Opik, Lunary, and OpenLIT, the last of which also powers Grafana’s AI-observability offering [56]. The second camp is the general-purpose observability backends that ingest GenAI telemetry over OTLP alongside ordinary logs, metrics, and traces: OpenObserve, Grafana/Tempo/Loki stacks, and Elastic. The choice between the two camps is a real architectural decision. The LLM-native tools have richer prompt and eval workflows. On the other hand, a unified backend avoids operating a second observability stack, and keeps the AI telemetry queryable next to the infrastructure telemetry that we need to correlate it with. This is essentially the argument of Majors and Carter [47] applied to deployment topology. Buyer’s guides consistently observe that the OTel-native tools (OpenLLMetry, Phoenix, OpenLIT, and OpenObserve) leave the most room to swap components later without re-instrumenting [62, 64]. 6.3 The frontier: leading practice in mid-2026 A few developments define the current edge of practice. All of them are ahead of anything in the academic literature. Agent runtimes that emit telemetry by construction. In April 2026, within one week of each other, Anthropic and OpenAI shipped hosted agent harnesses (Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI’s equivalent). The platform runs the agent loop, tool execution, sandboxing, and checkpointing, and exposes the whole run as a server-sent event stream. This changes where observability lives: it is no longer something the application developer bolts on, but something the runtime emits natively. Framework-level tracing (the OpenAI Agents SDK and LangGraph, see Section 8.3) was the precursor. Trajectory-level evaluation. Practice has shifted from scoring final answers to judging the path the agent took: whether the planner decomposed the task sensibly, whether the right tools were selected, whether the retriever returned stale context, and how many retries occurred. Platforms now ship trajectory-level scorers and session replay as standard features [63]. This is the industrial counterpart of the academic trace-analytics work in Section 8.2, and the industry demand here has run far ahead of the academic ability to automate the analysis. TRAIL’s roughly 11% error-localization result (Section 8.2) is the relevant reality check. Guardrails at full-traffic cost. Purpose-trained small judge models (Galileo’s Luna-2 line is the visible example) now score hallucination, toxicity, PII, and prompt-injection signals on all production traffic, at sub-200ms latency and at a cost that makes 100% sampling viable. This is a very different operating regime from GPT-4-as-judge on a 1% sample, and it blurs the old line between observability and control: the same component that records and alerts can now intercept and block. Frontier labs monitoring their own agents. The labs themselves have become the most demanding practitioners of agent observability, applied to their own systems. Starting from February 2026, METR ran a pilot exercise with Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, and OpenAI, in order to assess the misalignment risks from AI agents used inside the frontier developers [57]. Both OpenAI and Anthropic publicly report running automated monitors, i.e., LLMs prompted to review agent transcripts for harmful or risky actions, over the large majority of their internal agent traffic. OpenAI reports excluding less than 0.1% of agentic traffic from monitoring. The interesting thing for this review is the shape of the practice: transcript capture, automated semantic review, and escalation, at near-total coverage, all in support of a safety case. It can be expected that versions of these requirements will flow down to regulated enterprises over time. AI consuming observability data. The mirror image of observing AI is AI doing the observing. Datadog’s Bits AI SRE [61], which has been generally available since mid-2025, autonomously investigates alerts, reads telemetry and topology, follows runbooks, and proposes root causes. AWS shipped a DevOps agent in spring 2026 with case studies claiming around 77% MTTR reduction, PagerDuty’s Spring 2026 release puts an agent directly on escalation policies, and a crowded startup segment (NeuBird, Rootly, Anyshift, etc.) competes on the same premise. One effect is that telemetry is more and more designed for machine consumption, which raises the value of schema regularity and semantic conventions. Another effect is a recursion: the AI SRE agent investigating our outage is itself an agent, whose trajectory needs observing, evaluating, and guarding. 7. Evaluation as an Observability Signal The thing that most distinguishes AI observability from its predecessors is that output quality must be measured continuously, without ground truth, on live traffic. There is a substantial academic literature under this layer. For LLM-as-judge, Zheng et al. [11] is the methodological foundation. They showed that GPT-4 judges reach over 80% agreement with human preferences, which is comparable to human-human agreement, and they characterized the systematic judge biases (position, verbosity, and self-enhancement). Virtually every online-evaluation feature in the platforms of Section 5 and Section 6 rests on this result. An important corrective comes from Shankar et al. [18], whose EvalGen study identified what they call criteria drift: evaluation criteria cannot be fully specified up front, because they co-evolve with the observation of actual outputs. The implication for monitoring is that LLM-judge-based monitors need continuous human-in-the-loop recalibration; they cannot be deployed in a set-and-forget manner. On hallucination, the taxonomy of Huang et al. [14] maps out what quality monitoring needs to detect. Two detection approaches fit production settings particularly well. SelfCheckGPT [12] works black-box, via consistency across sampled responses, which matches the API-served-model situation that most deployments are in. Farquhar et al. [15] introduced semantic entropy, an uncertainty measure over clusters of semantically equivalent generations, and the follow-up semantic-entropy probes [16] approximate the signal from hidden states cheaply enough for runtime use. Guardrails sit adjacent to evaluation: runtime enforcement constrains behavior, and it also generates telemetry, in the form of policy-violation events that monitoring consumes. NeMo Guardrails [13] is the canonical open toolkit for programmable rails. Dong et al. [17] survey the guardrail landscape, and argue for a systematic socio-technical approach to building and verifying them. As noted in Section 6.3, industry has since pushed guardrails to full-traffic, sub-200ms operation using small purpose-trained judges, which is well past what the academic literature has characterized. Finally, an open-source ecosystem of evaluation frameworks connects offline evaluation to online observability through shared metric definitions. OpenAI Evals established the pattern of evals as code plus a shared registry. Ragas [53] contributed the standard reference-free RAG metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context precision/recall), which are now routinely scored over production traces. DeepEval covers CI-style regression testing, promptfoo covers adversarial red-teaming (and now sits inside OpenAI’s infrastructure, see Section 6.1), and MLflow’s GenAI tracing ties evaluation runs to OTel-compatible traces, so that quality failures can be root-caused span by span. Judging from the 2026 buyer’s guides [62, 63], the workflow that teams are converging on is to use the open-source frameworks for speed at the pull-request level, and the commercial platforms at the production level, where compliance and audit requirements bite. 8. Agent and Multi-Agent Observability The 2024–2026 shift from single-completion LLM features to autonomous, tool-using agents restated the observability problem once again. The unit of analysis is now a multi-step, non-deterministic workflow with planning, memory, tool calls, and inter-agent handoffs. 8.1 Taxonomies and failure modes Dong et al. [21] provide the foundational academic treatment, “AgentOps: Enabling Observability of LLM Agents”: a systematic mapping of AgentOps tooling that identifies the artifacts to be traced across the agent lifecycle (plans, tool invocations, memory operations, and guardrail events), motivated explicitly by AI-safety needs. Cemri et al. [24] contribute MAST, the first empirically grounded multi-agent failure taxonomy: 14 failure modes in three categories (system-design flaws, inter-agent misalignment, and task-verification failures), derived from more than 1,600 annotated traces across seven frameworks. Failure taxonomies like these function, in effect, as requirements specifications for what agent observability has to be able to surface. 8.2 Trace analytics and automated debugging Moshkovich et al. [22] argue that black-box benchmarking cannot characterize non-deterministic agentic systems, and propose analytics built from runtime logs (flow discovery and issue analytics), with follow-up work [23] framing a full observe-analyze-optimize loop. Deshpande et al. [25] introduce TRAIL, a benchmark of 148 human-annotated agent traces containing 841 errors under a formal taxonomy. The best evaluated model localizes errors with only about 11% success. This number quantifies how far automated root-cause analysis over agent traces is from practical reliability, and it should be kept in mind when reading the commercial AI SRE claims in Section 6.3. At the systems layer, AgentSight [26] demonstrates instrumentation-free observability via eBPF “boundary tracing”: it intercepts TLS-encrypted LLM traffic for semantic intent and kernel events for system effects, and causally correlates the two with under 3% overhead. The problem it addresses is the gap between what an agent says it is doing and what the operating system observes it actually doing, and to the best of my knowledge there is no other good solution to this problem yet. 8.3 Framework and protocol instrumentation On the practice side, OpenAI’s Agents SDK ships tracing on by default, with structured spans for model calls, tool calls, handoffs, and guardrail executions, plus pluggable exporters that third-party platforms consume [52]. LangGraph pairs deterministic graph execution with step-level state-transition traces and replay. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has surfaced a distinctive gap: MCP servers are opaque to the calling agent, which sees only the request and the final response, so tool-internal failures, cascading downstream errors, and retry loops are all hidden [56]. Active work includes an official proposal to propagate OTel trace context through MCP’s _meta mechanism [36], which is necessary because MCP transports such as stdio and WebSockets lack the HTTP headers that W3C Trace Context assumes, as well as OTel semantic conventions for MCP operations, which as of mid-2026 model each MCP invocation as a distinct tool span [32]. 9. Standards and Interoperability The defining development of 2024–2026 is the convergence on OpenTelemetry as the substrate for AI telemetry. The OTel Generative AI semantic conventions (gen_ai.*) [29], developed by a dedicated SIG since April 2024, standardize the schema for LLM inference spans (gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens, gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, and structured input/output messages), client metrics (operation duration, and token usage by type), and span kinds covering invoke_agent → chat → execute_tool hierarchies. As of semconv v1.41 (2026), the conventions cover agent, workflow, tool, and model spans plus the required latency and token-usage metrics, with parallel SIG work on agentic systems (tasks, actions, teams, and memory) and MCP [30–32, 65]. Note that the conventions remain in Development status, which means attribute names can still change without a major version bump, and the industry commentary through mid-2026 describes them as still stabilizing. Accordingly, they should be cited as an emerging standard. Nevertheless, the adoption is already broad: Datadog, New Relic, and Honeycomb consume them, and frameworks emit them natively or via instrumentation packages. Two open specifications preceded and shaped this effort. OpenLLMetry [34] provided OTel-compatible instrumentation for LLM providers, vector databases, and frameworks, and co-led the semantic-conventions working group. OpenInference [35] defines a complementary attribute schema, whose span-kind taxonomy (LLM, agent, tool, retriever, embedding, and chain) underlies Phoenix, and remains the principal alternative convention. MLflow Tracing documents explicit alignment with the OTel GenAI conventions, and Langfuse ingests OTLP natively. In other words, the ecosystem has effectively settled on OTLP as the interchange format, even while the attribute schema is still moving. The arrival of machine consumers of telemetry (Section 6.3) raises the stakes on getting the schema settled, since an AI SRE agent reading traces benefits from schema regularity even more than a human does. 10. Regulatory and Governance Drivers The last strand of literature turns observability from an engineering best practice into a compliance obligation. The EU AI Act [37] is the strongest driver: Article 12 mandates that high-risk AI systems technically enable automatic event logging over the system lifetime (minimum six-month retention, with per-use logging detail for biometric systems), and Article 72 requires providers to operate a documented post-market monitoring system collecting operational data. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile [38] define, through the MEASURE and MANAGE functions, what an AI observability program must be able to quantify, and catalogue twelve GenAI risks including confabulation, harmful content, and information-security failures. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 [39], the first certifiable AI management-system standard, requires monitoring, measurement, analysis, and evaluation of AI systems (Clause 9), which makes observability data audit evidence. Industry practice is already internalizing this. The frontier labs’ near-total transcript monitoring of internal agent traffic (Section 6.3) and the METR cross-lab pilot [57] show voluntary practice running ahead of the regulatory minimums at the top of the market, and the 2026 buyer’s guides consistently list audit and compliance requirements as what pushes enterprises from open-source tracing to commercial platforms. For regulated deployments, the tracing and logging capabilities surveyed above are simply not optional any more. 11. Synthesis and Research Gaps In this article, I have reviewed the literature and the industry progress on observability of modern AI application systems. A few themes run through both the literature and the industry record. The clearest one is continuity: AI observability is best understood as a composition of distributed tracing (from Dapper to OTel), ML monitoring (from technical debt to drift detection), and LLM evaluation research, with each strand supplying one layer of the stack. The second theme is that the trace is the unifying abstraction. Across academic and industrial work alike, the span tree of an LLM or agent execution is the data structure onto which everything else (cost, latency, payloads, eval scores, feedback, and safety signals) gets attached, and the loop from production traces to curated eval datasets to an improved system has become the standard workflow. The third theme is that continuous, ground-truth-free quality measurement is what actually separates AI observability from APM. Academically, this capability rests on LLM-as-judge, self-consistency, and uncertainty methods, each with documented reliability caveats; industrially, it has recently become cheap and fast enough (small judge models, full-traffic guardrails) to run inline. The fourth theme is standardization and consolidation: the field is standardizing on OTel/OTLP with the gen_ai.* conventions as the schema, while the vendor landscape consolidates into data platforms and regulation converts logging into a legal obligation. One more theme is new in this version of the review: the loop between the observer and the observed is closing, in the sense that agents now consume observability data (AI SRE), and agent runtimes emit it by construction (managed agent platforms). The open gaps relevant to a research project in this area are summarized as follows. There is no mature, peer-reviewed survey of the whole field. The closest candidates are the AgentOps taxonomy [21], MAST [24], and a non-peer-reviewed multi-layer synthesis [28]. A systematic multivocal literature review remains an open contribution, and the industry developments of Section 6 exist almost entirely in grey literature, which strengthens the case for the multivocal method. Automated root-cause analysis over agent traces is unsolved, despite being actively sold. TRAIL [25] puts the state-of-the-art error localization at about 11%, while commercial AI SRE products claim large MTTR reductions on infrastructure incidents. These are probably both true, because agent-trace debugging is a much harder problem than metric and log anomaly investigation, but reconciling them rigorously, and independently benchmarking the commercial claims, is open territory. Judge reliability and criteria drift. Online evaluation inherits the biases of LLM judges, and the criteria co-evolve with observed outputs [18]. Principled methods for calibrating and maintaining production monitors, including the small purpose-trained judges now used for full-traffic guardrails, are underdeveloped. Cost and overhead of semantic monitoring. Uncertainty methods like semantic entropy impose multi-fold inference costs. Industry’s answer is distilled sub-200ms judge models, which work in the sense of being deployed at scale, but whose reliability has no published characterization. Cross-boundary trace propagation for agents. Connecting agent-side and tool/MCP-server-side telemetry across non-HTTP transports is an open protocol problem, and so is correlating semantic intent with system-level effects (the AgentSight “semantic gap” [26]). Standards immaturity. The OTel GenAI, agent, and MCP conventions remain experimental as of mid-2026. The schema churn and the OpenInference/gen_ai.* split leave interoperability incomplete, at exactly the moment when machine consumption of telemetry makes schema stability more valuable. The privacy/payload tension. Effective LLM observability wants full prompt/response capture, while privacy regulation and PII exposure argue against it. Redaction and sampling strategies that preserve debuggability are largely unstudied academically. In practice, this tension is a main reason why the self-hosted stack (Section 6.2) persists. Observability of internal and frontier agent deployments. The METR cross-lab pilot and the labs’ transcript-monitoring practices are documented only in safety-community reports [57]. How those techniques (automated semantic review at near-100% coverage) transfer to enterprise settings, and what guarantees they actually provide, has not been examined.
